mcqs.question: A model achieves 99.8% accuracy on the training set. What can you conclude about its ability to generalize to new data?
options: It will generalize well, since high training accuracy reflects a well-fit model
It's definitely overfit, since accuracy above 99% is always a red flag
Nothing reliable — high training accuracy is consistent with genuine learning or with memorizing training examples, including their noise
It generalizes well as long as the dataset is large
mcqs.explanation: Training accuracy alone can't distinguish a model that learned the true pattern from one that memorized training examples and their noise — both look equally good on data they were trained on. Only performance on withheld data reveals which happened. High training accuracy by itself isn't proof of overfitting either — it depends entirely on how the model does elsewhere.

mcqs.question: While tuning a model, should you check test-set accuracy after each hyperparameter change to decide which change to keep?
options: Yes — the test set gives the most reliable signal to guide tuning decisions
No — training accuracy should be used for tuning decisions instead
Yes, as long as you only check it a few times
No — every decision made based on test performance makes the test set stop measuring generalization and start measuring fit to itself
mcqs.explanation: The test set's value comes entirely from staying untouched until the final check. Using it to guide any decision — even 'just checking' occasionally — lets information from it leak into your choices, so the final reported number stops being an honest estimate. Tuning decisions belong to the validation set, not the test set or raw training accuracy.

mcqs.question: Why does k-fold cross-validation generally give a more reliable performance estimate than a single train/validation split, especially on a small dataset?
options: Every row gets used for validation exactly once across the k runs, so the final score is an average rather than depending on one lucky or unlucky split
It trains a bigger, more accurate final model
It automatically removes any data leakage from the pipeline
It reduces the total amount of data needed to train a model
mcqs.explanation: A single split's score can swing a lot depending on which rows happened to land in validation, especially with little data. Averaging over k folds, where every row is validated on exactly once, smooths out that variance. K-fold doesn't fix leakage or shrink data requirements — it's purely about the stability of the estimate.

mcqs.question: A churn model includes a feature that records how many support tickets a customer filed 'in the week leading up to cancellation' — but this field is only ever populated once a customer has actually canceled. What type of problem is this?
options: Class imbalance — cancellations are rare
Overfitting — the model has too much capacity
Target leakage — the feature can only exist because the outcome already happened
A stratification error from not splitting by outcome
mcqs.explanation: A feature that can only be computed once the label is already known — here, it requires knowing a cancellation happened — lets the model 'predict' using a disguised version of the answer. This is target leakage, unrelated to model capacity, class balance, or how the split was stratified.

mcqs.question: A team fits a StandardScaler on the entire dataset, then splits into train and test afterward. What's wrong with this order of operations?
options: Nothing — scaling doesn't depend on the split, so order doesn't matter
The split should always happen before any data is loaded into memory
StandardScaler should never be used with cross-validation
The scaler's mean and variance are computed using test-set rows, leaking test-set statistics into the training pipeline
mcqs.explanation: Fitting a scaler on the full dataset means its computed statistics are influenced by rows meant to be held out. The fix is to fit the scaler only on the training split, then apply that same fit unchanged to validation and test. This is preprocessing leakage — subtle, but a common real-world bug.

mcqs.question: You're building a model to forecast next week's demand from two years of daily sales history. Which splitting strategy is correct?
options: A time-based split — train on earlier dates, validate and test on later dates, with no shuffling
Standard k-fold cross-validation with shuffling, for the most stable estimate
A random hold-out split, since demand forecasting is a regression problem
Stratified k-fold, since demand values are imbalanced across days
mcqs.explanation: Time-ordered data needs a split that respects the order: training on the past and validating on the future mirrors how the model will actually be used. Random hold-out or shuffled k-fold would let the model train on future dates and validate on the past, leaking information that wouldn't exist in production. Stratification addresses class imbalance, not time order.

mcqs.question: A dataset has 2% positive (fraud) examples. A random 80/20 split is used without stratification. What's the risk?
options: The model will always overfit to the majority class
Random splits always preserve class ratios automatically, so there's no risk
The validation set could end up with very few or zero fraud examples, making the reported score unstable or meaningless
The training set will end up with duplicate rows
mcqs.explanation: With a rare class, a plain random split can by chance concentrate most of the few positive examples on one side, leaving the other with too few — or none — to evaluate reliably. Stratified sampling avoids this by splitting each class separately so its ratio is preserved everywhere. It doesn't inherently cause overfitting or duplicate rows.

mcqs.question: A time-series forecasting model shows strong validation accuracy using a shuffled random split, but performs far worse after deployment. What's the most likely cause?
options: The model architecture is too simple for the deployment data
The learning rate was set too high during training
The validation set was too small
Shuffling before splitting let the model train on data from after the point it was validated on, leaking future information
mcqs.explanation: Shuffling destroys time order, so training data can end up from dates after the validation dates — the model effectively got to peek at the future, inflating validation scores in a way that can't hold once deployed on genuinely unseen future data. The fix is a strict time-based split with no shuffling.

mcqs.question: You tune a model's hyperparameters using 5-fold cross-validation, then report the best fold's score as the model's expected real-world performance. What's wrong with this?
options: The reported score is optimistically biased, because the same folds used to pick the best hyperparameters are also used to report the final score
Nothing — cross-validation already prevents any leakage
5 folds is too few; only 10-fold results are trustworthy
The issue only applies to deep learning models, not simpler ones
mcqs.explanation: Picking the hyperparameters that scored best on a given set of folds, then reporting that same score, means you've implicitly selected for whatever did best on that exact data — an optimistic bias. Nested cross-validation fixes this with an outer loop held out purely for the final score and an inner loop that does the tuning. Fold count and model type don't change this structural issue.
